paras: The attempted lynching of John Griffin and attack on Black residents of Shawneetown took place in Shawneetown, Illinois, between August 31 and September 3, 1903, when a masked mob tried to take Griffin, a Black prisoner accused of an attempted assault on a white woman, from the jail, and whites then stoned Black homes and gathering places. The jailer held off the mob and the sheriff moved Griffin to the jail at Carmi; no one was reported killed or hurt, but at least fifty Black residents left the town within two days. Wire stories carried the episode to white papers from Virginia to Wyoming and to two Black weeklies.

Griffin, described as "colored," was under arrest for an attempted assault on Mrs. Joseph Hobbs, a white woman, near her home; according to the first dispatch her screams frightened him away and he was arrested a short time afterward. A Shawneetown dispatch said ill feeling had existed among "a class of white men" against Black residents for several months. Passengers quoted by the Paducah Sun added that the town had "recently inherited a large crowd of stray negroes" after the Danville, Illinois, and Evansville, Indiana, race riots.

Late on Monday night, August 31, or about 2 a.m. Tuesday, a mob of masked men, fifty in most reports and forty-five in one, demanded that Jailer Galloway hand over Griffin. Galloway reasoned with the men from the jail door, then armed himself and warned that anyone who tried to force the jail would do so at his peril. The mob made several failed attempts to break down the doors and dispersed about daylight.

Many Black residents took Griffin's side, and according to one version of the wire they said he had been drunk, had only frightened the woman, and should not be put to death. Others left for fear of a race riot; passengers reaching Paducah said Black residents were leaving on every boat and some on foot.

The mob prepared a second attempt on the jail, or by another account returned, but Sheriff Mills had already taken Griffin to the jail at Carmi for safekeeping. Whites then raided the Black quarter and stoned houses, "resorts and dives" where Black residents gathered, on Tuesday night according to one report and on the night of September 2 according to another. Many Black residents fled to friends in the country, and a September 3 dispatch counted fifty driven out in forty-eight hours. No bloodshed was reported, and the local authorities were said to be taking every precaution against a riot.
The last reports placed Griffin in the Carmi jail, and the coverage does not show a trial, any arrests among the mob, or the return of those who had left.

White papers ran the foiled jail attack under headlines such as "Illinois Mob Is Foiled," then the driving out under "War at Shawneetown" and "War on the Black People." The first dispatches spoke of an "attempted assault," while the later wire called Griffin "a negro who had attacked a white woman." The Washington Times headed the exodus "Negro in Illinois Persona Non Grata," and the Converse County Herald in Wyoming called those who fled "the more cowardly ones."

The Paducah Sun, the nearest paper in the coverage, blamed the tension on Black residents "inciting hot-headed white people by openly siding with the negro in jail." By contrast, the Springfield Weekly Republican praised Galloway for facing down a "niggerhunting" mob, crediting the Danville sheriff's example, but said nothing of the stoning.

In the Black press, the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate printed both wires on September 3, under "Run Negroes Out of Town" and "Jailer Faces Crowd and Prevents Negro from Being Hanged—Race War in Illinois Town." The Baltimore Afro-American followed on September 5 with the full jail dispatch as "Town in Fear of a Race Riot," its subhead ending "Colored People Flee." Neither paper added comment, and the Advocate kept the wire's statement that Griffin had attacked the woman.
The first dispatches said Griffin attempted an assault and was frightened off, later wires said he "made an attack," and Black residents were quoted as saying he was drunk and only scared the woman.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Griffin and attack on Black residents of Shawneetown
bases: A masked mob went to the jail to take and lynch Griffin and failed (A1, A7, A5); the same mob then stoned Black houses and gathering places and drove out about fifty Black residents (A6, A13, A4), a community attack that grew out of the attempted lynching.
The jail attack is reported in two separate wires (A1, A7) and an independent passenger report (A2), and the stoning and exodus in two separate dispatches (A4, A6/A13).

accounts.label: First wire (Shawneetown, Sept. 1)
accounts.gist: Fifty masked men demanded Griffin, held for attempted assault on Mrs. Joseph Hobbs; Jailer Galloway armed himself and the mob dispersed at daylight after failing to break in; Black residents sided with Griffin and some left.

accounts.label: Second wire (Shawneetown, Sept. 2)
accounts.gist: Forty-five masked men attacked the jail at 2 a.m.; Jailer 'Calloway' held them off alone; Black residents said Griffin was drunk and only scared the woman, and a race riot was feared.

accounts.label: Steamboat passengers (Paducah Sun)
accounts.gist: Black residents were leaving on every boat and on foot; the town had wanted to be rid of Black newcomers from the Danville and Evansville riots, and Black residents had provoked whites by siding with Griffin.

accounts.label: Driving-out wire (Sept. 3-4)
accounts.gist: The mob, disappointed in its effort to lynch Griffin, raided the Black quarter, stoned houses, resorts and dives, and drove fifty Black residents out in 48 hours; the mob returned but Sheriff Mills had moved Griffin to Carmi.

accounts.label: Ill-feeling dispatch (Sept. 3)
accounts.gist: A class of white men had felt ill will against Black residents for months; the stoning followed the jail attack, at least fifty left, and the authorities guarded against a riot.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wires under headlines such as 'Illinois Mob Is Foiled', 'War at Shawneetown' and 'War on the Black People', stating the accusation as fact in the later version ('a negro who had attacked a white woman').
The Paducah Sun called the newcomers 'stray negroes' and blamed Black residents for 'inciting hot-headed white people' by siding with Griffin.
The Washington Times headed the exodus 'Negro in Illinois Persona Non Grata' and '"Colored Brethren" Driven in Herds'.
The Springfield Weekly Republican praised Jailer Galloway for facing down a 'niggerhunting' mob and credited the example of the Danville sheriff, without mentioning the stoning.

The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran both wires ('Run Negroes Out of Town'; 'Jailer Faces Crowd and Prevents Negro from Being Hanged') and the Afro-American the first jail wire ('Town in Fear of a Race Riot'), without comment and keeping the wire's statement of the accusation.
